strengths: Well-motivated and clearly presented analysis establishing that self-supervised speech (SS) representations linearly predict EMG power (r=0.85), with the notable finding that the low-dimensional D(E) (22 dims) outperforms the much higher-dimensional spectrogram feature vec(B) (991 dims) for both unit and phoneme decoding.

Systematic and rigorous empirical study across multiple SS models (HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, WavLM) and all layers, producing interpretable layer-wise correlation curves and connecting the HuBERT layer-6 peak to prior observations about optimal resynthesis layers.
Principled formulation of EMG as SPD covariance matrices and their diagonal/geodesic geometry, with a clear and reproducible description of the TDS-Conv + CTC pipeline and feature construction.

Addresses a real data-scarcity problem by constructing a substantially larger corpus (~9 hours, ~6,800 unique words, 115 wpm) than prior EMG-to-speech work, with an explicit commitment to open-sourcing data and code.

The gesture-separability analysis (70.6% with D(E), 73.7% with the full covariance) is a clean, above-chance demonstration that EMG power encodes discriminative articulatory information, and the use of an independently collected gesture dataset strengthens the claim.
Alignment-free CTC formulation is appropriate for the unknown-alignment setting, and the paper is generally well-written and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim — end-to-end EMG-to-speech synthesis — is not supported by any evaluation of the synthesized audio. There is no WER/CER, no MOS or listening test, no objective intelligibility metric, and no spectrogram/audio comparison. The authors themselves state in Section 6 that perceptual evaluation is ongoing future work. The title and abstract therefore promise a result that the evidence does not deliver, which is a fundamental gap between claims and support.
The reported error rates (PER ~41%, UER ~59%) are far too high to characterize the output as usable 'speech synthesis'; the framing overstates the maturity of the system.

The motivating linear-mapping analysis and the actual synthesis system are logically disconnected: the r=0.85 correlation is computed on D(E) as a proxy for vec(E) (footnote 4), whereas the decoder operates on vec(E)/D(E)/vec(B) and decodes dis(H)_HuBERT units — the strong linear relationship is never the mechanism actually used, weakening the paper's narrative that the analysis 'motivates' the pipeline.
The claim of synthesis 'without vocoder training' relies on a pretrained Tacotron vocoder; the architectural novelty relative to prior unit-to-speech pipelines is modest.

No comparison to prior EMG-to-speech systems or to ground-truth audio; all comparisons are internal to the authors' own feature choices (vec(E), D(E), vec(B)), so relative contribution is hard to gauge.

Reproducibility cannot be verified: data and code are stated to be released only 'upon completion of the project,' and no artifacts are available at review time. Given that the corpus is a central claimed contribution, this is a material concern.

The finding that SS models encode articulatory/kinematic information is already established in prior work [24, 25]; the extension to EMG power is incremental, and the novelty is not clearly delineated from those results.
Statistical rigor is limited: only standard deviations are reported, with no significance testing, and Figure 2's separability evidence is shown for a single subject only.

The gesture-classification dataset (12 subjects, 13 gestures, 10 reps) is small and separate from the speech corpus, so the articulatory-separability claim and the speech-decoding claim rest on different, unevenly validated data.

strengths: The paper reports a clean and interesting empirical observation: self-supervised speech representations (HuBERT, Wav2Vec 2.0, WavLM) can be linearly mapped to the diagonal of the EMG covariance matrix D(E) with a Pearson correlation as high as r = 0.85. This is a concrete, testable finding about what SS models implicitly encode.

The layer-wise analysis (Figure 3) is a nice piece of interpretability work. The observation that the peak correlation for HuBERT-base occurs at layer 6 — the layer previously identified as optimal for discrete speech resynthesis and spoken language modeling — provides a mechanistic interpretation of a known empirical result and is a genuine, if incremental, contribution.

The gesture clustering analysis (Section 5.1, Figure 2) is well-motivated and supports the claim that both E and D(E) encode discriminative articulatory information, with k-medoids accuracy (70.6% / 73.7%) well above the 10% chance level.
The paper is generally well-written, the figures are clear, and the architecture (Figure 5) is easy to follow. The ethical statement is appropriate and detailed.

If the promised large-vocabulary EMG corpus (9 hours, ~6,800 unique words, 115 WPM) is in fact released, it would be a valuable resource for the community, since prior work is limited to small-vocabulary, low-rate corpora.
weaknesses: The central claim of the paper — the title and abstract promise 'synthesizing speech' and 'end-to-end EMG-to-speech generation' — is not supported by any evidence. No synthesized audio is presented, and there is no objective or perceptual evaluation of audio quality (no MCD, no WER/CER on synthesized speech, no MOS). The 'Continuing work' section explicitly states that methods to assess perceptual quality and compute WER/CER are still being developed. A paper whose headline contribution is speech synthesis but which provides no synthesis results has a fundamental gap between its claims and its evidence.

The results that are reported (Tables 1 and 2) are intermediate metrics with very high error rates: UER of 58.7–64.2% for predicting HuBERT discrete units and PER of 41.4–53.8% for phoneme decoding. No baseline from prior EMG-to-speech work is provided for comparison, and no demonstration is given that these error rates could yield intelligible speech. The relative ordering of vec(E) > D(E) > vec(B) is the only supported conclusion, but all absolute numbers are poor.

The pipeline itself closely resembles the prior alignment-free work it claims to improve upon ([6, 2]): predict discrete HuBERT units from EMG/neural signals via CTC and feed them to a pretrained vocoder. The claim of doing so 'without explicit articulatory models and vocoder training' is misleading — a pretrained Tacotron vocoder is still used. The claimed methodological novelty relative to [2, 6] is therefore unclear.

The link between the headline linear-mapping result (H → D(E), r = 0.85) and the actual synthesis system is weak. The authors acknowledge that the inverse direction (D(E) → H) is ill-posed and non-invertible in the linear case, yet they use the forward-direction result as the main motivation for a nonlinear EMG→H pipeline. The logical connection is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is currently limited. The footnote states that data and code 'will be made publicly available upon completion of the project,' so the resource and pipeline are not actually available at review time, and the paper is explicitly framed as 'Continuing work,' suggesting it is incomplete.

Some of the broader framing overstates novelty: prior work ([24, 25]) has already argued that SS models infer articulatory kinematics. The contribution here is a specific linear-probing instantiation of that idea, which is interesting but incremental.

strengths: Targets an important and challenging problem: non-invasive EMG-to-speech for individuals with speech impairments, with potential clinical and accessibility impact.

Introduces a methodologically interesting representation for EMG using SPD covariance matrices and Riemannian/Cholesky geometry, and uses it to probe self-supervised speech models for articulatory information.

Makes a serious data-collection effort: a large-vocabulary (~6,800 words, ~9 hours) EMG corpus at natural speaking rate (~115 wpm), addressing a key limitation of prior small-vocabulary/private datasets.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with helpful figures (e.g., electrode placement, pipeline) and a clear exposition of the proposed feature representations.
weaknesses: The central claim of synthesizing speech from EMG is not supported by any synthesis results. The paper reports only unit error rate (UER) and phoneme error rate (PER) for intermediate targets; there are no synthesized audio samples, no intelligibility metrics (WER/CER), and no perceptual evaluation. Section 6 explicitly states that objective assessment of perceptual quality and WER/CER are future work. Thus the title and abstract overstate the demonstrated contribution.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Data and code are not released; they are only promised 'upon completion of the project.' Critical details are missing: number of participants in the speech corpus, per-subject splits, alignment/timestamping procedure between EMG and audio, TDS architecture hyperparameters, linear probing regularization, and training details. The IRB protocol number and conflict-of-interest statement are blank.

There are no comparisons to prior EMG-to-speech methods or appropriate baselines, despite claiming to address the limitations of prior work. The only comparisons are among the authors' own feature representations (vec(ℰ), D(ℰ), vec(B)), with no ablation of the TDS network, rotation-invariance module, or CTC objective, and no statistical tests for reported differences.

The evidence for the central probing claim (H linearly maps to D(ℰ), r=0.85) is potentially confounded. D(ℰ) reflects overall muscle activation power, which correlates with vocal effort/loudness; no control is provided for speech amplitude, overall EMG activation, or shuffled/random features. Pearson correlation on concatenated time-series may also be inflated by autocorrelation and slow shared trends.

The abstract links H → linear mapping → D(ℰ) → gesture-specific clustering → articulatory movements, but the gesture clustering experiment (Section 5.1) uses a separate non-speech dataset of 13 orofacial movements from 12 participants, while the linear mapping experiment (Section 5.2) uses the speech corpus. No experiment shows that D(ℰ) predicted from H preserves the gesture-specific clustering structure or that these clusters correspond to speech articulatory mechanisms.

There are serious internal inconsistencies in dimensionality. Section 3 describes 31 EMG data electrodes; Section 5.1 uses 22 electrodes for gesture data; Section 5.3 says D(ℰ) is 31-dimensional; Table 2 claims both vec(ℰ) and vec(B) have 991 dimensions, which is incompatible with either 22 or 31 electrodes and 31 frequency bands. These errors make the setup hard to reproduce and undermine confidence in the results.

The reported performance is very poor for a speech synthesis system: 58.7% UER for HuBERT units and 41.4% PER for phonemes with the best input. No evidence is provided that such outputs yield intelligible speech, and no error analysis or oracle/random baselines are given. The paper does not establish a usable EMG-to-speech interface.

Claims that other EMG features (log-spectrograms, rectified signals) 'cannot be directly probed' to reveal structured articulatory representations are asserted but not experimentally validated. A comparison of clustering/decoding on those features is needed to support this argument.

The 'end-to-end' and 'without vocoder training' framing is misleading. The pipeline uses a frozen pretrained HuBERT and a frozen Tacotron vocoder; the system is not trained end-to-end, and no end-to-end evaluation is performed. The contribution is an intermediate unit-prediction pipeline, not a demonstrated synthesizer.

The paper reads as an incomplete work-in-progress. The 'Continuing work' section admits that core evaluations are not yet done. This is not yet a complete, publishable contribution under ACL/ARR criteria.

strengths: Releases substantial open-source resources: a large-vocabulary ~9h EMG-speech corpus from a healthy speaker and a ~1h corpus from a participant with ALS, plus code and detailed appendices, which materially improves reproducibility over prior private-data EMG-to-speech work.

Presents an interesting and well-supported empirical finding: a simple linear map from S3 representations (HuBERT/Wav2Vec2/WavLM) to EMG power D(E) achieves r=0.85, and orofacial gestures form separable clusters under covariance-based features (k-medoids 61-74% vs 7.7% chance), supporting the articulatory-structure interpretation.

Principled, interpretable, and articulatorily motivated design (covariance/SPD representations, geodesic distance, shift-tolerant TDS encoder) that is simple to implement and effective in low-data regimes, with clear architecture and training details in the appendix.

Addresses the clinically meaningful and harder alignment-free setting (no frame-level EMG-audio correspondence), and includes a phoneme-guided decoding scheme with a consistency loss that gives a statistically significant UER reduction.
Comprehensive evaluation suite: probing analysis across model families/layers, ablations on training data size and losses, human WER/PER, MOS, and a comparison to an EMG-to-text variant.
weaknesses: The headline synthesis results are weak: WER of 62.55% (healthy) and 50.82% (ALS) and UER ~56%, which limits practical utility despite the authors' contextualization against invasive BCI baselines.
Generalization evidence is very limited: a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant, so claims about broader applicability (laryngectomy, dysarthria) are not empirically supported.

Gains from phoneme-guided decoding are modest (UER 56.08 -> 51.81), and the core synthesis pipeline relies on a frozen pretrained vocoder whose contribution is hard to disentangle from the proposed encoder.

The central 'S3 encodes articulatory mechanisms' claim rests on a correlational linear probe; the mapping is high-to-low dimensional and could partly reflect speaker/prosodic factors rather than articulatory structure, so the interpretive leap is somewhat stronger than the evidence directly warrants.

No direct one-to-one comparison to prior EMG-to-speech methods is possible (acknowledged), and the ALS WER being lower than the healthy-speaker WER is left unexplained, raising questions about corpus/vocabulary effects.
MOS is computed on only 35 sentences with 10 raters, and the reported 3.79 value, while reasonable, provides limited perceptual evidence for the quality of the synthesized speech.

strengths: Open-sources a large EMG-to-speech dataset, including a healthy participant (~9 hours, 6,800+ words) and an ALS participant (~1 hour, 300 words), which is a valuable community resource for non-invasive speech interfaces.

Provides a rigorous and novel analysis showing that self-supervised speech (S3) representations linearly predict EMG power with correlation up to r=0.85, and identifies layer 6 of HuBERT as particularly aligned with articulatory structure, offering mechanistic insight into why layer 6 is useful for speech resynthesis.

Demonstrates that covariance-based EMG features form separable clusters for distinct orofacial gestures, with k-medoids accuracy substantially above chance (61.41% for diagonal power, 73.7% for full covariance).

Introduces a phoneme-guided decoding approach with a consistency loss that improves unit error rate over a unit-only CTC baseline (e.g., 56.08% to 51.81% on the healthy dataset; 52.29% to 46.98% on ALS), with reported statistical significance.

Presents an alignment-free EMG-to-speech pipeline that avoids frame-level EMG-audio alignment and trains an encoder to predict discrete HuBERT units, using widely available pretrained components (HuBERT, Tacotron vocoder).
Evaluates intelligibility with human transcribers (WER) and perceptual quality with MOS (mean 3.79), and reports unit/phoneme error rates averaged over multiple random seeds.
Provides strong reproducibility: detailed architecture, hyperparameters, data splits, electrode placement, training objectives, and links to code/data/audio demonstrations.

Addresses a clinically relevant problem with ethical approval, participant consent, and a clear limitations section that acknowledges single-participant scope, distribution shift, and long-term stability concerns.
Contextualizes WER with prior invasive brain-computer interface studies, helping readers interpret the results in the appropriate clinical and sensing context.
weaknesses: The synthesis evaluation is limited to a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant; there is no cross-participant or longitudinal generalization evidence, which limits confidence in the broader applicability of the method.

For the healthy participant, the synthesis targets are derived from gTTS audio rather than the participant's own recorded speech, even though subject-recorded audio is available. This likely underestimates achievable performance and weakens direct comparison to methods that use paired EMG-audio data.

Word error rates remain high (62.55% on the healthy large-vocabulary set and 50.82% on the ALS set), and direct EMG-to-speech underperforms the cascaded EMG2TEXT pipeline (51.17% WER with a language model), limiting demonstrated practical utility.

No external baseline is run on the proposed dataset because the unaligned setting lacks existing benchmarks; the comparisons are mainly internal feature ablations (vec(B), D(E), vec(E)) rather than direct comparisons to prior EMG-to-speech systems.

The claim that phoneme-guided decoding improves generated audio quality is supported primarily by unit error rate reductions, but not by a controlled MOS or WER comparison against an otherwise identical model without phoneme-guided decoding.

The unit-to-phoneme mapping model reports 0% phoneme error rate on the test split, which is surprisingly perfect and not analyzed in depth; this raises questions about the reliability of the lookup table used in the consistency loss.

The "open-vocabulary" characterization is not fully substantiated: test sentences are held out, but word overlap with training vocabulary is not quantified, and no evaluation on entirely unseen words is provided.

Several design choices, such as using gTTS targets for the healthy participant and relying on a pretrained vocoder, are not ablated, making it difficult to isolate their impact on the reported performance.

strengths: Genuine, lasting data contribution: the paper open-sources DATA_GENERAL (~9 h, ~6,800 words), DATA_ALS (~1 h, ~300 words, ALS participant), and DATA_OROFACIAL_GESTURES (12 subjects, 13 gestures). Publicly available EMG-to-speech corpora are scarce, and these resources can support reproducible follow-up work.

Reproducibility is a clear priority: project page, GitHub, data links, released synthesized test audio, human transcripts, and detailed implementation notes (electrode placement, filtering, model hyperparameters, WFST decoding). This is well above the norm for the area.

The alignment-free pipeline (frozen S3 model + TDS convolutional encoder + pretrained vocoder, trained with CTC on HuBERT units) is a reasonable, simple-to-implement design, and the demonstration that phoneme-guided decoding with a consistency loss improves UER (56.08 → 51.81, Table 3) is statistically supported (p < 10^-6) across 5 seeds.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough for a small-N study: multiple seeds with error bars, human WER/PER from three transcribers (Fig. 9), MOS from 10 raters (Fig. 10), and an appendix WFST-based emg2text comparison. The authors are candid about the high absolute error rates and contextualize them against invasive BCIs.

The gesture-clustering analysis (Fig. 1; k-medoids 61.41% on D(E), 73.7% on E vs. 7.69% chance) provides direct evidence that covariance/diagonal EMG features carry discriminative articulatory information, independent of the speech pipeline.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim is overclaimed. A linear map from H (768–1024 dims) to D(E) (31 dims) is a heavily overparameterized regression; a high held-out r=0.85 is not strong evidence that S3 models 'implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms.' Both H and EMG are driven by the same phonetic content (and likely by the same energy/envelope dynamics), so the correlation is confounded. The only control provided is mel-spectrogram A → D(E) (r=0.61), but A has 80 dims vs. 768–1024 for H, so dimensionality/capacity is not matched. No control using random or untrained features, and no test that the mapping survives after regressing out energy, is reported.

The layer-wise 'principled interpretation' (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 2) is an overreach: the correlation curves are nearly flat (roughly 0.83–0.86 across layers), so the asserted alignment of HuBERT layer 6 with an 'optimal resynthesis layer' is reading signal into noise. The claimed convergence of evidence is not warranted by the data shown.

Evaluation of the actual contribution (synthesis) rests on two participants (one healthy, one ALS). The ALS result has no ground-truth audio, is scored only by human transcription, and uses a ~300-word vocabulary, making the reported 50.82% WER difficult to interpret or generalize. The healthy-subject WER of ~62% (Table 5) is high, and MOS 3.79 is moderate. No longitudinal or cross-session robustness is shown, as the authors acknowledge.

The 'end-to-end EMG-to-speech generation' framing is misleading. The system is a two-stage pipeline (EMG → discrete HuBERT units → pretrained Tacotron vocoder), and the supervision target is HuBERT units of gTTS audio derived from the ground-truth transcript. It is not end-to-end, and the vocoder is pretrained, not trained; 'without vocoder training' is a weak claim since all the acoustic modeling is inherited from the vocoder.

No direct, controlled comparison against prior EMG-to-speech systems. Comparisons to Gaddy & Klein, Littlejohn et al., and Metzger et al. are relegated to Appendix C and explicitly declared non-comparable; EMG2QWERTY is a keyboard-typing baseline. As a result, the reader cannot assess whether the proposed design is actually better than simpler alternatives.

The empirical advantage of the proposed covariance representation is incremental. vec(E) (56.08 UER) vs. vec(B) (62.71) is a real but modest gain, and D(E) with 31 dims matches vec(B) with 961 dims, which the authors use to argue for structured features — yet this could equally reflect that the spectrogram baseline is weak. The claimed benefit of 'articulatorily grounded' features is therefore not decisively established.

There is a potential circularity in the phoneme-guided decoding: the lookup table P(phoneme | unit) is estimated from a GRU trained on DATA_GENERAL (the same corpus used for synthesis), and the consistency loss then enforces agreement with this self-derived table. The paper does not analyze how much of the gain is due to genuine articulatory structure vs. self-distillation from in-domain statistics.

The paper claims the datasets are 'one of the largest and most comprehensive publicly available resources,' but the ALS set (1 h, ~300 words) is small and the healthy set (~9 h) is single-participant; the claim of broad utility would be better supported by at least a second healthy speaker or cross-speaker results.
